title: Superconducting diode effect from field-induced $s+if$ pairing in Ising superconductors
abstract: The in-plane critical field of Ising superconductors exceeds the Pauli limit by an order of magnitude because the Ising spin-orbit coupling locks the electron spins out of the basal plane. The same locking converts an in-plane Zeeman field into a source of equal-spin triplet Cooper pairs, so that the field-driven condensate acquires an $s+if$ character. We show that this conversion channel also generates Lifshitz invariants, the odd-in-momentum terms of the Ginzburg-Landau expansion responsible for the superconducting diode effect. When the basal mirror symmetry of the monolayer is lifted by a substrate or a gate, the field-induced triplets couple linearly to the Cooper-pair momentum, and an intrinsic diode response develops whose strength is set by the ratio of the Zeeman and spin-orbit energies rather than by the small ratio of the spin-orbit and Fermi energies familiar from parity-mixing mechanisms. We construct the symmetry-constrained two-component Ginzburg-Landau theory of the coupled singlet and triplet order parameters and derive all of its coefficients from the microscopic model of an Ising superconductor; the complete functional, including all gradient and quartic terms, is generated by a single pair-breaking function of temperature, field, and Cooper-pair momentum. An attractive triplet channel reshapes the diode response: at weak fields it suppresses the efficiency through destructive interference between the direct and the collective-mode conversion paths, while at strong fields it extends the diode regime well beyond the singlet-only critical field, with the maximal efficiency reached along the triplet-enhanced phase boundary. The diode effect thereby serves as a transport probe of a hidden triplet pairing channel and of the field-induced $s+if$ state.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes the superconducting diode effect in Ising superconductors due to field-induced s+if pairing. By developing a two-component Ginzburg-Landau theory, the authors demonstrate that the SDE is governed by the coupling between singlet and triplet channels. This effect provides a novel transport measurement to detect the presence of hidden triplet pairing states.
main_problem: The paper investigates the superconducting diode effect (SDE) arising from field-induced s+if pairing in Ising superconductors.
main_result: The SDE is shown to be a transport probe for the hidden triplet pairing channel, with the diode response strength controlled by the ratio of Zeeman to spin-orbit energies ($\Delta Z/\Delta 	ext{so}$).
method: The authors construct and analyze a symmetry-constrained two-component Ginzburg-Landau theory for coupled singlet and triplet order parameters, deriving coefficients from a microscopic model.
model_or_system: The system is an Ising superconductor (e.g., monolayer TMDs) subjected to an in-plane magnetic field, which induces an s+if condensate character via triplet Cooper pairs.
key_observables: Superconducting Diode Effect ($\eta_{	ext{SDE}}$), Lifshitz invariants, and the superconducting order parameters ($\psi$ and $\mathbf{d}$).
important_parameters: Zeeman energy ($\Delta Z$), spin-orbit energy ($\Delta 	ext{so}$), and the ratio $\Delta Z/\Delta 	ext{so}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the GL theory framework and the assumption that the triplet sector can be integrated out to yield an effective single-component theory.
figures_summary: Figure 3 illustrates the temperature and field dependence of the diode efficiency, showing the triplet channel extends the diode regime beyond the singlet-only critical field.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical mechanism (SOC leading to triplet pairing and Lifshitz invariants) to constructing the full GL theory, deriving effective coefficients, and finally analyzing the resulting SDE behavior under varying field strengths.
why_interesting: The strong coupling between magnetic fields, spin-orbit coupling, and superconducting symmetry breaking provides a rich platform for studying emergent quantum phenomena in condensed matter systems, relevant to understanding topological superconductivity.
